1.pericope_label: God's answer to Moses: now shalt thou see what I will do

schools.summary: Calvin thinks Moses unworthy of so kind a reply, and reads the Father of all goodness as pardoning the sins of leader and people alike that he might effect the deliverance he had determined; in the phrase now shalt thou see he hears a tacit reproof of an impatience that would not wait for the result of the promise. He explains why God refused a voluntary release: the work of liberation was to be conspicuous, and the words drive them out are to be pressed, since the king who today refuses will not merely consent but expel Israel from his kingdom and count their speed a blessing. Gill notes only that the word answered the questions and expostulations Moses had put.

Henry fixes the moment: Moses was at his wit's end, wishing he had stayed in Midian rather than come to Egypt to make bad worse, and now that the affair had reached a crisis, Pharaoh at the height of pride and Israel in the depth of misery, it was God's time to appear — man's extremity being God's opportunity, and the church's deliverance accomplished when God takes the work into his own hands. He turns the strong hand to use, that as some are brought to their duty by the strong hand of grace, made willing in the day of God's power, so others by the strong hand of justice, which breaks those that will not bend. Because his account of the whole message is filed at this verse, he sets out five grounds of comfort in it: the name, which is one with I am that I am, the fountain of being and infinite perfection, a God who performs what he has promised and perfects what he has begun, and who in the creation history is never called Jehovah until the heavens and the earth are finished, his people meanwhile finding him El-shaddai; the covenant, which God not only makes but establishes, as firm as his power and truth can make it; his compassion, since he notices the increase of his people's calamities; the resolutions themselves, line upon line, where man may take the shame of an unbelief needing such repetition and God the glory of the grace that grants it; and the intention behind them, double, their happiness in being taken for a peculiar people and his own glory in being known for the Lord. That such words did not revive them he accounts for three ways: they were too taken up with their troubles to heed Moses, too cast down by the late disappointment to believe him, and too afraid of Pharaoh's wrath to stir towards their own deliverance.

Clarke observes that the Hebrew here uses the verb elsewhere translated to harden, and takes the strong hand for sovereign power suddenly and forcibly applied: God would display his power before the Egyptians, and Pharaoh in consequence would display his own by thrusting the people out.

Ellicott states the complaint the verse answers — Moses had charged God with delay, with being slack concerning his promise, and with not delivering his people at all — and reads now shalt thou see as an assurance that there will be no more delay, the work being about to begin, so that Moses will behold it and cease to doubt. He would render the phrase through a strong hand rather than with it, meaning the compulsion God exerts.

2.pericope_label: I am Jehovah: the name, the older name, and the covenant recalled

schools.summary: Gill takes the declaration for a summary of the divine nature — the self-existent Being, the everlasting I am, unchangeable and constant to his promises — makes El-shaddai God all-sufficient, having a sufficiency of happiness in himself and enough for his creatures' wants, and holds the covenant sure and never to be made null. Calvin reads the speech as a rebuke of distrust by way of the covenant: God advances nothing new, since the people had almost imbibed the doctrine of their adoption with their mother's milk, so their complaint against Moses, as though he had invented what he promised in God's name, is less pardonable; and the comparison stings, since Abraham, Isaac and Jacob embraced the promise and trusted it perseveringly while their descendants disdained it because fulfilment did not appear at once. On the older name he canvasses the etymologies without settling them, holding that where God engages himself to Abraham under it he promises to be merciful and bounteous, the respect being to loving-kindness rather than might in judgment. He makes the patriarchs' tolerated wandering their praise — exemplary virtue to live all their lives with no corner to set a foot on but what neighbours allowed for a tent, in a land the covenant had made their inheritance — which condemns the posterity that would not go up to it; and he explains the long delay, that God would have them sorely troubled to succour them more openly and unjustly oppressed to rescue them more justly, since had the laws of hospitality been kept there had been no cause to shake off the yoke. God's remembering, he adds, means the showing of it by what he does.

Clarke insists on the rendering I am Jehovah, since without the proper name the next verse's reason is not obvious, and calls El-shaddai the dispenser or pourer-out of gifts. The denial that the fathers knew the name he treats as a crux, since it occurs from Genesis onward and God had used it of himself to Abraham, and he canvasses four solutions before giving his own: that the name was known from the first but what it implied was not, a man being able to bear the title of an office long before he does any of its work. On the covenant he has God now fully purposed to give effect to all his engagements. Wesley glosses the name as a God who gives being to his own promises, and refers the groaning to the late hardships.

Ellicott traces El-shaddai from Abraham through Isaac to Jacob, finding its primary idea in overpowering strength, against which the idea of Jehovah is absolute, eternal, unconditional existence. He renders the disputed clause was I not made manifest to them, and defends the name's antiquity from a derivation out of a form already obsolete in Moses' day, from its presence in the oldest documents taken up into Genesis, and from Abraham's use of it in a place-name; why the stress shifted he explains historically, the patriarchs needing assurance that God could perform, whereas Israel stood in closest contact with polytheism and had partly fallen into it, the Existent meaning the Self-Existent and so the Only Existent, a standing protest against every other god. The next phrase he renders the land of their sojournings wherein they sojourned, Canaan having been occupied by sufferance, the ownership reckoned the Canaanites'.

6.pericope_label: The seven promises, and why Israel would not hear them

schools.summary: Gill grounds the promises in the name that heads them — eternal in being, immutable in counsel, faithful to his covenant and able to fulfil it — and explains the taking of a people two ways, politically, that out of Egyptian hands they should be his kingdom and subjects, and religiously, that they should be a holy people to fear and serve him by rules given from himself, both effected by the setting up of a civil and an ecclesiastical polity. Calvin presses the promise past the departure: it would have been little that the people should once be redeemed unless they then lived under God's guardianship, and having long since set the holy seed apart by circumcision he sets it apart again, so that both their election and its perpetuity are asserted, to be accounted God's people being to be received by special privilege into his favour and called by adoption to the hope of eternal salvation. Canaan he treats as the earnest of that adoption, the fathers' faith not being tied to earthly blessings; and on the lifting up of the hand he adds that the gesture cannot properly be said of God, who swears by himself because there is none greater, there being more than enough steadfastness in his simple word, so that the oath is a concession to human weakness. That the people would not hear he finds marvellous rather than natural: no wonder men intoxicated with prosperity reject God's mercy, but sorrow ought to awaken longing, and instead the afflicted harden against the promises — so we should struggle to get our minds clear enough of grief to receive grace.

Clarke identifies the promise as the covenant made with Abraham, then asks why God should take so refractory and worthless a people for his own, and answers three ways: because he had promised their ancestors, in general friends of God; because, as Warburton observes, the providence protecting them was the more visible for their want of shining qualities, which might otherwise have let the effects be ascribed to their own wisdom; and because God would show that he delights to save the lost, choosing the worst people in the universe to prove that he wills not the death of a sinner. He agrees with Calvin that the lifting up of the hand is the gesture of an oath. On the failure of the message he says their labour was so continual and their bondage so cruel they had scarcely time to breathe, and notes that the Samaritan adds a sentence here, let us alone that we may serve the Egyptians, borrowed from a later chapter. Wesley reads the stretched-out arm as almighty power, a metaphor from a man stretching his arm out to put forth all his strength.

Ellicott notices that the idea of God redeeming Israel appears here first, and that the redemption was accomplished twice over — by the wonders culminating in the tenth plague, whereby they ceased to be Pharaoh's slaves and became God's servants, and by the passage of the Red Sea, which delivered them from death and so purchased them anew. He guards the other side of the election: the choice of a peculiar people did not mean abandoning the rest, since God continued to govern all nations and in every nation accepted those who feared him, a principle the centurion and Cornelius carry into the Gospel. On the failure of the message he contrasts the two announcements, the first having elated them with a hope they had long been strangers to, while by now they had been chilled by disappointment, their leader's interference having only increased their misery. Keil fixes the Hebrew closely: it is shortness of breath, meaning not impatience but anguish, an inward pressure that stops a man breathing properly, so that the early belief changed into the despondency of unbelief as the oppression grew, and it spread to Moses, who declined his commission again.

10.pericope_label: The second sending, the uncircumcised lips, and the charge

schools.summary: Gill has the orders renewed at another time, remarks that access to Pharaoh seems not to have been difficult, and observes that the objection is passed over, having been sufficiently answered before, with Aaron joined in the charge. Calvin measures the forbearance in the renewal: the just reward of so malevolent a repulse would have been to let the people rot in their miseries, and it is of God's extraordinary loving-kindness that he does not cease helping those willing to perish. The new command was needed to strengthen Moses, shaken by the people's despair and concluding he was to go no further; his objection Calvin sets out as an argument from the less to the greater, since it would be harder to move Pharaoh against his will than to persuade the afflicted to accept help offered from heaven, and if the people's hearts were a closed door, why try to shift the exceeding great rock? Moses did not design to throw off his calling, but so the heartiest of God's servants faint midway, where the path proves worse than they expected. The summarising verse he renders the Lord had spoken, referring it back to the calling's commencement, to show that the brothers had not acted rashly but on command, and that however often the work was interrupted God's purpose held. The uncircumcised lips he refers to the stammering already pleaded.

Henry, whom Wesley abridges here, draws the rule that God repeats his precepts before he begins his punishments: those called in vain to leave their sins must be called again and again, whether they will hear or forbear, God being said to hew sinners by his prophets, which denotes the repetition of the strokes. He finds two pleas in the objection. The first is the unlikelihood of Pharaoh's hearing: if the anguish of their spirit makes Israel deaf to what would comfort them, much more will pride make him deaf to what can only exasperate him — and if God's professing people will not hear his messengers, how shall his professed enemy? The second is the infirmity of speech, already sufficiently answered, so Moses ought not to have pressed it, the sufficiency of grace supplying nature's defects. The charge he reads as God ending the dispute by interposing his own authority: when Moses repeats his baffled arguments he is argued with no longer but charged upon his allegiance, God's authority sufficing to answer all objections and binding men to obey without murmuring or disputing.

Clarke takes the word rendered uncircumcised to signify anything exuberant or superfluous, and would have rendered it protuberant lips had Moses not been remarkable for his beauty; as it is he refers it to a want of ready utterance, from a defect in the organs of speech or a knowledge of Egyptian impaired by forty years away.

Ellicott notices that the second message advances on the first: the first asked only leave to go into the wilderness, much of which lay within Egypt's limits, the second that Israel be let go out of the land — such, he says, being the way of Providence, since refuse a light cross and a heavier is laid on, and decline the Sibyl's first offer and she brings a worse bargain the second time. On the lips he reports Rosenmüller's argument that Moses was tongue-tied, but doubts more is meant than the slowness of speech alleged earlier, uncircumcised standing by Hebrew idiom for any imperfection interfering with efficiency, an uncircumcised ear being one that cannot hearken, an uncircumcised heart one that fails to understand. The summarising verse he makes a seam: the details stand at the opening of the next chapter, which he thinks originally followed the objection directly, this verse being added to summarise them when the genealogy was inserted. Keil takes it instead for a concluding summary preparing for the genealogy headed in the next verse, and cites Ranke as having proved its organic connection with the narrative so conclusively that even Knobel gave up the fragmentary hypothesis.

14.pericope_label: The genealogy: why it stands here, and how far it can be trusted

schools.summary: Calvin puts the purpose sharply: the leader's origin is testified to all ages so none may doubt the promise to Abraham was fulfilled in the departure, since under any other leader it might have been questioned who the chief author was; and because Satan has obscured this history through profane writers, labouring to bury the race of Abraham, Moses anticipates him by naming the heads of families. The fewness of sons he takes for proof of a miracle: that three men so long-lived begat so few did not happen without design, so that in the fecundity which followed the miracle of grace might appear the clearer, God seeming first to mock their contemptible beginnings and then showing his power in their multiplication. He notes too what Amram's marriage cost the narrator, since nature itself, before ever the law forbade it, dictated that a man should not take his aunt, who stands to him in a mother's degree, and Moses in confessing it proclaims his parents' disgrace for the glory of God — from which we learn that imitating the patriarchs indiscriminately is not safe. Gill reports the opinion that the three tribes are noticed to show they were not rejected though rather cursed than blessed by Jacob, but prefers the plainer account, that the first two are named for the third's sake.

Henry calls it no endless genealogy of the kind the apostle condemns, since it ends in Moses and Aaron and shows them Israelites, bone of the bone of those they were sent to deliver, raised up of their brethren as Christ also should be. He reports Lightfoot's view that Reuben, Simeon and Levi are dignified here because their dying father had left them under marks of infamy, Reuben for his incest and the other two for the murder of the Shechemites, so that Moses would magnify God's mercy in their repentance; but he too prefers the plainer account, that order might be kept and the deliverers of Israel plainly appear Israelites. On the ages he and Wesley agree that Moses came far short of the fathers and fixed seventy or eighty for the ordinary stretch of life, since now that Israel was a great nation and revelation was written rather than trusted to tradition, the two great reasons for the patriarchs' long lives had ceased.

Clarke makes the genealogy a proof that the two came in a direct line from Abraham, and calls the whole passage a parenthesis that does not belong to the narration. He adds from Dodd that Levi is thought to have outlived all Jacob's sons, surviving Joseph by twenty-seven years though much the elder, and finds the promise of deliverance in the fourth generation verified exactly, Moses being son of Amram, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Jacob.

Ellicott sets the pedigree in its culture, genealogies holding as prominent a place among Arabians as among Jews, a would-be leader's descent being matter of curiosity to all who submitted to him. He denies that the list can be complete: ten generations at least stand between Jacob and Joshua, so three between Jacob and Moses are scarcely possible, and the Israelites habitually built genealogies by dropping links, as the pedigrees of Ezra and of our Lord show. He reckons four or five names omitted between Kohath's son Amram and Moses' father Amram, and presses the numbers — Gershon had but two sons, Kohath four and Merari two, yet the Levites numbered twenty-two thousand three hundred males the year after the Exodus, an increase requiring some ten or eleven generations. Keil explains the form: a father's-house is a technical term for a body of families called by a common ancestor, and the list begins at Reuben to fix Levi's place, naming only such sons of the first two as founded families.

17.pericope_label: The Levite line, and the return to the charge

schools.summary: Gill holds Jochebed to have been Amram's aunt, since Numbers says expressly she was a daughter of Levi born in Egypt, though the Vulgate, Septuagint, Samaritan and Syriac all make her his uncle's daughter, as does Polyhistor after Demetrius. He thinks Izhar's sons named for Korah's sake, a remarkable history following in the next book, and canvasses three views of Putiel — Lightfoot's, an Egyptian convert, perhaps of the stock of Potipherah among whom Joseph had sown true religion; the Targum of Jonathan and Jarchi, who make him Jethro; and Aben Ezra, whom he prefers, an Israelite whose name cannot now be explained. On the emphatic naming he reports the puzzle that Aaron stands first here and Moses first in the next verse, with Aben Ezra accounting for it by Aaron's seniority and his prophesying in Egypt first, Jarchi taking the reversal to show them equal, and Gill himself allowing that the historian may simply not have cared. The last verse he treats as a bare repetition. Calvin seizes the word armies for a contrast between the armies of a nation and two abject men who could never have borne so weighty a burden had God not worked through their hands beyond every hope: what was less probable than that a multitude enough to make many nations should obey two men and migrate against a powerful king's will? What no earthly king could effect with all his terror, God did by two unwarlike men, one of whom kept deprecating the commission. He notes an ambiguity in the closing verses, which might mean that God spoke in Midian and then in Egypt after some time elapsed, though he prefers to take the three together.

Clarke goes with the versions against Gill on Jochebed: the word is of uncertain force, Parkhurst showing it serves for an uncle and also for an uncle's son, and the Vulgate elsewhere rendering it my paternal cousin, so that the best critics suppose her a cousin-german and not an aunt. He observes that though Korah became a rebel, Moses in his impartiality set the name among his own progenitors; construes Elisheba as the oath of the Lord and makes her sister to Nahshon; takes the armies for regularly arranged troops in battalions, whence God has the name Lord of hosts; and would begin the seventh chapter at the resumption, the sixth ending completely at the naming of the two. Wesley draws the rule that Levites might marry into any tribe, no confusion or loss of inheritance following, and answers the renewed objection from the charge itself — speak all that I say unto thee, as a faithful ambassador, for those who go on God's errand must not shun to declare his whole counsel.

Ellicott needs no softening on the marriage: unions with aunts and nieces were not unlawful before the Law, and were common throughout the East and at Sparta. He adds that Korah's sons did not share his sin and so did not die with him but headed important families, that Amminadab and Naashon stand among David's ancestors and so appear in the genealogies of our Lord, Naashon being prince of Judah at the Exodus, and that the term armies is used of Israel here first, referring it to the quasi-military organisation given during the struggle with Pharaoh, which let them leave Egypt not a disorderly mob but in array.
